One domain per site. A binding is provisional until its TXT ownership record proves it: another site can take an unproven one over, and it lapses after 24 hours if DNS never pointed here (7 days in any case). A proven domain is exclusive (`409 domain_taken`). A name another site on this server already serves cannot be connected. Each account may ask for at most 5 new domain certificates a day; the sixth waits. Sites that are taken down, and suspended accounts, get no domain checks. [[hosted]]`simple-hack.app` and the service's own zones cannot be connected.[[/hosted]]
Enterprise has no custom domains by decision; Simple Hack team sites live on the event's hosts; on a small box the server's own web front issues a connected domain's certificate on demand.

The family answers site labels only; the bare suffix itself is not routed to your home page or showcase, and the wildcard certificate does not cover the apex. Nothing is served until both records are seen; a pending family is dropped after 24 hours. Several accounts may wait on one name; the first to prove it wins and the others are emailed. A verified family is exclusive: no other account can connect it, an overlapping family, or a custom domain under it. The label `www` never names a site. The wildcard certificate is set up by the operator; until then the status says waiting for the operator. If it fails every check for a day, the account is emailed. After three days the domain is disconnected and must be connected again with the TXT record. [[hosted]]`simple-hack.app` and the service's own zones are refused as suffixes.[[/hosted]]

value.title: Simple Hack
value.line: Simple Hack runs hackathons from sign-up to results, team sites included. It is the same software run as its own product.

features.name: Run an event
features.line: Create a hackathon at simple-hack.app, move it through its stages with one button, add co-organisers, and delete it when done.
features.who: Organisers, from a single person running a weekend event to a team of co-organisers.
features.how: Sign in at https://simple-hack.app and create an event; it gets its own public page at `<event>.simple-hack.app`, a join link, a judge link, and a code of conduct. The Overview shows one forward button for the current stage (open, building, closed, judging, results, ended), worked out on the server so the website and your AI app agree; moving to Results also locks judging. You can invite co-organisers with one seven-day link that anyone can accept until you revoke it, rename teams, download participant, team, entry, and score CSVs, download every team site as an archive, and see storage use. Settings ends with Delete this event, which asks you to type the event's address name and then removes the public page, results, entries, scores, votes, member access, custom website, and storage for good. A standing demo event on simple-hack.app lets you try the participant and judge paths from https://simple-hack.app/watch.
features.example: A university society creates its spring hackathon, adds two co-organisers, walks the Overview button from Open to Results over the weekend, and exports the results CSV for the prize ceremony.
features.where: simple-hack.app, Manage (Overview, People, Settings), or ask your AI app with the organiser role.
features.limits: On simple-hack.app, three new events per account per day and five active events per organiser; admins and listed accounts have no limit. Self-hosted installs have no active-event limit by default. The event creator cannot be removed. There is no undo and no email after deleting an event, and the address stays reserved once anyone has joined. Moving a stage backwards asks for confirmation.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server; the weekly demo event is hosted only.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 L1811-1834 (M0/M1 status, stages), Env row EVENT_CREATE_PER_DAY (20; 0 = no limit), EVENT_MAX_ACTIVE_PER_ORGANISER (0 = no limit), and EVENT_LIMIT_EXEMPT (admins and listed accounts are never limited), 'Delete an event', 'Event administration', 'Event page Look', 'Organiser Overview', 'Weekly demo reset' (hosted deploy/prod script, hence hosted only). PARITY rows 'Hosted hackathon platform', 'Simple Hack Manage and one button system'.

features.name: Registration, applications, tracks, and announcements
features.line: People join by link or apply from the public listing; organisers ask sign-up questions, set tracks and prizes, and post announcements.
features.who: Participants joining an event, and organisers deciding who gets in and keeping everyone informed.
features.how: Participants join with the event's link, or, for an event listed in Find a hackathon, apply from the listing or the event's public page without a link. Applications are on by default and every application waits for an organiser's decision in People, Applications; an applicant may add a city, country, age range, and gender, which stay with that event and are never shown to other organisers. Organisers can ask up to eight text questions at sign-up and require approval; pending and rejected applicants see their own status. Up to twelve tracks each carry a challenge and a prize, and each team picks one track before its deadline. Organisers publish sponsors, an FAQ, a schedule with time zones, and announcements, can edit or delete an announcement, and can email participants, send a receipt on a team's first complete entry, and show a public submission countdown. The schedule shows the real times on its own (event start and end, the entry deadline, the voting window, results), so they never drift, and a schedule row can ask the organiser for the next step when its time comes, for example “Kickoff is now. Open sign-up?” It never moves the stage itself. Participants see “Demos starts in 12 minutes” on their Home.
features.example: A company running a public AI hackathon lists it in Find a hackathon, takes applications over two weeks, approves 80 people, and announces the final schedule by email the night before.
features.where: Find a hackathon and the event's public page for applicants; Manage (Settings, People, Content) for organisers; or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Only listed events take applications; unlisted events are join-link only. Five applications per account and 30 per IP address each hour, 20 pending applications per account, and 500 pending applications per event. A rejected applicant can apply again only after withdrawing. Editing an announcement does not send a new email. Track names may repeat; removing a chosen track warns how many teams lose their choice.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Applications without a join link' (limits 5/account, 30/IP per hour, 20 pending, 500 per event), 'Registration, tracks and challenges', 2026-10-27 track and announcement notes, 'Leave this event' (rejected applicant withdraws and may apply again, superseding 'cannot re-apply'). PARITY row 'Event content and communications'. 'Outgoing mail visibility' is an operator-side mail journal and daily watch with no user-visible surface; covered silently.

features.name: Teams
features.line: Find teammates, ask to join or invite, run your team as its admin, lock it, share its link, and leave an event cleanly.
features.who: Participants forming and running teams, and organisers filling the gaps.
features.how: Solo participants see open teams with their track, room left, and members, ask to join, or list themselves with a short intro; team members invite listed people and accept or decline requests. Whoever creates a team is its first admin; admins approve requests, rename the team, edit its looking-for note, remove members, make other admins, lock or unlock the team, and roll a new team link (`https://simple-hack.app/team/<code>`), which anyone can preview before joining. Locking clears pending requests and invites and takes nobody new. Organisers can preview Fill teams, which places solo people into teams with room and then makes new teams, and apply it after confirmation. Anyone can leave an event from their Overview, Settings, or Home row menu, or through their AI app; before the team deadline an emptied team is deleted with its entry and site, and after it the team, its entry, its site, and its scores stay as they were. Any team member can message the organisers from Team; teammates and every organiser share the thread. Organiser Home shows unread team messages with Read and reply; opening the team clears the line for that organiser.
features.example: A designer with no team lists herself with a one-line intro on Friday evening; a team of three invites her, their admin approves, and the organiser runs Fill teams on Saturday morning for everyone still solo.
features.where: The signed-in team step on the event page; Manage, Teams for organisers; or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Team finding is private to approved participants and can be turned off per event, which hides the lists and stops new requests while codes still work. The looking-for note and solo intro are 120 characters. Team size defaults to 20 per event. Full teams cannot invite or accept, and a frozen team never takes a member back. The last admin cannot be removed until someone else is admin. A judge who leaves keeps their scores counting unless an organiser removes them; the event creator must name a successor before leaving. Team messages are 1 to 1000 characters, at most 10 per team per rolling hour, and stop after End. Organiser emails follow the Account preference, at most once per 15 minutes, when mail is set up.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Team finding', 'Teams redesign' (team size default 20, EVENT_TEAM_SIZE_DEFAULT), 'Leave this event'. PARITY rows 'Simple Hack: leave an event', 'Simple Hack: team admins and links', 'Hosted hackathon platform'. Contradiction: the §15 Env table row still lists EVENT_TEAM_SIZE_DEFAULT (4); the 2026-10-31 prose says 20 and wins. Standalone v0.8.13 carries team finding; the 2026-10-31 teams redesign and leave are not stated for the standalone package. 'Notify people when something waits on them' (2026-11-02): Needs you on Home, Overview and Home across events, sidebar badges, emails at most once per kind per 15 minutes, Account opt-out, hack_get_my_todos. 'Team messages' (2026-11-05): an organiser can message one or up to 25 teams at once; the team sees it in app and by email, with its own sent-message history. 'Teams write to the organisers (SIM-443)': any team member can write from Team. Both sides share a thread; organiser Home links unread team messages to Read and reply.

features.name: Entry card, rules and submit
features.line: Every team hands in the same short summary card, organisers decide what a complete entry needs, and a team submits when it is ready.
features.who: Teams finishing their entry before the deadline, and organisers who want every entry in the same shape for judges.
features.how: The card asks for the problem, the solution in one line, who it is for, the track, tools and AI as tags, and what works today, plus show-your-work evidence: a video, the team website, a code link or a screenshot. Organisers pick a preset (AI build, Coding, Ideas and design) or set each line Required, Optional or Off, and the evidence lines also One of; before saving tighter rules they see which teams it affects. Saving a draft never checks anything. Submit does, on the server, the same way on the website and in the AI apps. Home shows a four-step checklist and a countdown to the team's own deadline. At the deadline a complete draft is submitted automatically; an incomplete one is still judged, marked Incomplete, and the organiser can exclude it by hand. At each of the event's own reminder times before the deadline (24 hours and 1 hour by default), teams whose entry isn't submitted get a reminder email naming what is missing. Published results show each shown team's card on the public page.
features.example: An organiser picks the Coding preset, so a code link becomes required. A team fills its card, adds its repo and a video, presses Submit and sees the checklist on Home tick over.
features.where: Entry and Home for teams, Entries and the entry detail for organisers, in the Simple Hack app; hack_submit_entry and hack_set_entry_rules in the AI apps.
features.limits: Rules can change only until entries close. Tighter rules never un-submit an entry. A team that never started an entry is not judged.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Reminder times' (2026-11-05): one list of offsets (up to 5, 15 minutes to 14 days each, default 24 hours and 1 hour) drives both this entry reminder and the judging reminder, organiser-editable on Entries.

features.name: Judging
features.line: A weighted rubric, judges spread openly, automatically, by hand, or by track panel, conflicts of interest, a lock, and published results.
features.who: Judges scoring from a phone, and organisers running the rubric, assignments, and results.
features.how: The organiser sets a rubric of 1 to 10 criteria, each with a weight and a points scale, before judging opens; a new event starts with Idea, Execution, Design, and Demo at 25 percent each, scored 1 to 5. Judges are spread openly (everyone scores everyone), automatically (an even, conflict-aware spread), by manual assignment, or by panels per track. A judge or an organiser can declare a conflict of interest, which drops that pairing from queues and totals. Organisers, including co-organisers, can also judge under their own account, with the same conflicts and locks. The judge's queue puts the least-covered team first, the scoring screen opens the frozen team site and saves criteria as you go, and Save and next moves on. The organiser watches coverage on the dashboard, locks judging, then publishes: ties are flagged and can be resolved by hand, totals can be raw or normalised across judges, and public ranks and scores can each be hidden. After publication each team privately sees its total, rank, and the judges' comments without names.
features.example: A corporate innovation day with 30 teams and 9 judges uses automatic assignment, a sponsor's engineer declares a conflict with the team he mentored, and the organiser publishes winners only.
features.where: Manage, Judging for organisers; the judge link and Judge entries for judges; or ask your AI app with the judge role.
features.limits: Scoring opens at Judging, which locks mode, judges per team, rubric and assignments and generates Automatic assignments. Returning to Entries closed pauses scoring and unlocks setup. Rubric weights must sum to 100; the rubric cannot change while judging is locked, and removing scored criteria or lowering points below saved scores asks for confirmation. Unlocking requires a reason, which is logged. Automatic assignment includes organisers only with include_organisers=true on the API. Public results never show individual judge scores or comments. Results CSV and scores CSV can be downloaded at any time.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Judging (M3)', 'Judging choices', 'Organisers can also judge', 'Judging fixes' (confirmation on scored criteria, judges-only default, scoring opens at Judging), 'Archive cleanup' (default rubric). PARITY rows 'Hosted hackathon platform', 'Simple Hack Manage and one button system' (judging-first Manage). Standalone v0.8.9 carries judging-first Manage. 'Judge notices' (2026-11-05): judges are told in app and by email when judging opens and, while they still have teams to score, before it closes.

features.name: People's choice voting and the directory
features.line: A public vote on the entry gallery with one vote per verified email, and a public directory where organisers list their events.
features.who: Organisers who want a crowd prize, voters, and people looking for a hackathon to join.
features.how: Once the entry gallery is open, an organiser opens voting with a start and end time and chooses who may vote: any signed-in account, approved event members, or approved participants only. Each verified email has one vote per event and can change it until voting closes; counts and the ranking appear on the public vote page only after the close. The public directory at Find a hackathon groups events as happening now, upcoming, or past; new events are unlisted until an organiser opts in, and listing is also what lets people apply without a join link.
features.example: An accelerator demo day lets any signed-in person vote for a crowd favourite during the two-hour showcase and reveals the tally on stage at the close.
features.where: Manage, Judging (voting settings) and Settings (directory listing) for organisers; the event's public vote page and Find a hackathon for everyone.
features.limits: Voting opens only after the gallery. A voter cannot vote for their own team, including through a `+tag` email alias, which shares the one vote. Narrowing who may vote removes votes that no longer qualify, after confirmation. Only live gallery entries can be chosen. Draft and taken-down events do not appear in the directory. The tally stays after team sites are removed.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'People's choice and directory', 2026-10-27 review (confirm_vote_removal), 'Applications without a join link' (only listed events take applications). PARITY row 'Simple Hack sign-up, stages, voting and directory fixes'. Standalone availability not stated for voting; read as the same binary.

features.name: Team sites and the event website
features.line: Every team gets a site at its own address, published from an AI app or a zip; organisers can swap the built-in event page for a custom one.
features.who: Teams publishing their project, and organisers who want the event page to be their own.
features.how: Each team's site lives at `<team>.<event>.simple-hack.app`. A team publishes it from the AI app they already use (the connector selects the team, then the ordinary site tools publish) or by uploading a zip of static files with `index.html` at the root from the team's Publish card; both show the published address and version. Team sites use the same KV, SQLite, and file storage presets as any Simple Host site, with page recipes for the setup code, and saves can notify through webhooks. The event's public page is built in; an organiser can instead publish a custom website to the event address, versioned, with the latest five versions shown, and switch back to the built-in page at any time. An organiser can take a team site down and restore it. After an event is archived, team sites stay up for 30 days; the organiser gets one email 14 days before they are removed, and the event page and results stay.
features.example: A fintech team describes their prototype to Claude, which publishes the pitch page, demo, and a sign-up form to their team address; the organiser publishes a custom event site with the agenda and sponsor logos.
features.where: The team's Publish card on the event page, Manage, Page for organisers, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Team sites allow 25 MB of deployed files with two versions kept. Entries freeze at Judging, including for teams with extra time, so a frozen site cannot be changed. The team site's zip upload is rate limited per IP address and checks freezes and take-downs first. Write to support@simple-host.app for more time after the 30-day window.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server, where team sites live at `team.event.your-domain` and KV, SQLite, and files share a 1,000,000-byte allowance per site
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 L1806-1814 (zip uploads, versions, latest five), M2 status (team sites, take-down), 'Archive cleanup' (30 and 14 days), Env row MAX_ARCHIVE_MB=25 and KEEP_VERSIONS=2, 2026-10-27 review (zip limiter, freezes), 'Stage and entry fixes' (freeze at Judging), 'Personal connector parity' (select team then generic site tools). hackathons.html L96-101 (addresses, 25 MB, two versions, 1,000,000-byte allowance). PARITY rows 'Hack event websites and icon', 'Hosted hackathon platform'; webhooks from v0.8.11 release note.

features.name: The AI connector and skills
features.line: One connection at https://simple-hack.app/mcp works for organiser, participant, and judge roles, with skills for each.
features.who: Anyone who would rather run, join, or judge an event from the AI app they already use.
features.how: Connect your AI app to `https://simple-hack.app/mcp` once; the same personal connection lists the tools for every role and every event you are in, and the roles come from your membership, so an organiser who also judges needs nothing extra. Participants pick their team and then publish its site with the ordinary site tools. The event tools follow the same rules as the website, so membership, validation, and refusals match. Get started walks through five AI connector setups and offers a one-line install of the five-skill toolkit (run-hackathon, join-hackathon, judge-hackathon, and the site skills); the skill files are also downloadable. The role films on Watch include copyable prompts for creating an event, judging, and building a team site.
features.example: An organiser asks ChatGPT to create the event, set a rubric, and generate assignments; a judge asks Claude for their queue and scores from the train; a team asks Grok to publish their pitch page.
features.where: Get started at https://simple-hack.app/get-started, then your AI app.
features.limits: Tools ask before destructive or outward actions (opening events, replacing scored rubrics, publishing results, emailing participants, deleting people, teams, or events). Simple Hack accounts have no personal site address. A self-hosted instance's connector and skills point at that instance's own domain.
features.editions_note: Available as the standalone Simple Hack package on one server, with its own Get started naming its own connector
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Personal connector parity', Skill row (run-hackathon), 'Role films and standing demo' (copyable prompts), standalone v0.8.9 (self-hosted Get started names its own connector). PARITY row 'Hack agent toolkit' (five-skill hack-toolkit install, five connector setups). hackathons.html L85-86. Lead is marked 'implementing' in FEATURES.md but PARITY says deployed; treated as live.

features.name: Simple Hack inside a company
features.line: The whole platform on one Docker server, or on your Kubernetes cluster with your own Postgres, with company sign-in.
features.who: Companies running internal hackathons on their own network, and anyone who wants their own instance.
features.how: Download the standalone package (ZIP or tar.gz) and run the install on one Linux server with Docker and 2 GB of RAM; it brings the app, PostgreSQL, and a Caddy web server, with a persistent settings file, volumes for the database, sites, and certificates, and an upgrade script. Event pages use `event.your-domain` and team sites `team.event.your-domain`. People sign in through the company's OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak) with email sign-in turned off, or with email sign-in and optional Google. On an internal address the installer can issue certificates from its own CA, from the company's ACME server, or use the company's certificate files, and trust the company root. The page at https://simple-hack.app/companies explains the setup with a 45-second film and the two one-line install commands; DigitalOcean and Coolify guides cover those paths. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart in deploy/kubernetes runs the same image as one pod with your Postgres, a persistent volume for the sites and a TLS-terminating load balancer in front; the pod builds the database schema itself on first start, event pages use `event.your-domain` and team sites `event.your-domain/team/`, and docs/kubernetes.md is the runbook.
features.example: A bank's platform team installs Simple Hack on an internal VM behind Okta, runs a three-day hackathon for 80 engineers, and keeps every team site inside the network.
features.where: https://simple-hack.app/companies, the self-host page at /hackathons, and the standalone guide in the repository.
features.limits: You need a server, your own domain with apex and wildcard DNS, and a verified email sender unless company sign-in replaces it. Back up the database and site files before upgrades. The standalone package is Docker Compose on one server; the Kubernetes chart runs one pod (its upload locks and rate limits are in-process), so it scales up, not out. Hosting costs are your provider's bill; the hosted service at simple-hack.app is free.
features.editions_note: This feature is the standalone Simple Hack package itself (v0.8.13); the /companies page and its film are served by simple-hack.app

features.name: Role films and the standing demo
features.line: Three short drawn films show the organiser, judge, and participant paths, with a live demo event you can join or judge right away.
features.who: Anyone deciding whether to run or enter a hackathon on Simple Hack, before signing in.
features.how: https://simple-hack.app/watch plays an Organizer, a Judge, and a Participant film, six scenes each, with narration on click, pause and restart, draggable scene marks, mute, and keyboard controls; captions sit under the picture on a phone. Each film comes with copyable prompts for your AI app. Below the films, the page shows join and judge links for a standing demo event, so you can try the participant or judge path without making an event of your own. The home page and the companies page open with click-to-play films of their own.
features.example: A community organiser watches the organiser film, joins the demo as a judge to see the scoring screen on her phone, and then creates her own event.
features.where: https://simple-hack.app/watch, linked from the Simple Hack home page.
features.limits: The demo links appear only while the demo event is open or building and not taken down. The films and the demo exist on simple-hack.app only; a self-hosted instance does not serve them.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §15 'Role films and standing demo' (hosted-only /watch, demo JSON and redirects, self-hosted 404), 'Weekly demo reset'.

features.name: Ask about this event
features.line: Organisers can ask a small assistant on Home about their event; it answers in a line or two and links to where to act.
features.who: Organisers setting up an event who want to know what a setting means or what is left to do.
features.how: Press Ask on Home and type a question. The answer comes from the event's own settings and checklist, the app's screens and the docs, streams in as it is written, and links to the place to change things. When it isn't sure it says so and links the closest setting or docs page. It never changes the event. Chats stay in your browser, per event. Participants and judges don't have it.
features.example: Two weeks before kickoff, an organiser asks "Is my setup done?" and gets "Not yet: choose what teams hand in" with a link to Settings, Entries.
features.limits: 30 questions per organiser per day and a monthly budget for the whole service on simple-hack.app. Self-hosted installs turn it on by setting an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (ASSISTANT_BASE_URL, ASSISTANT_MODEL, ASSISTANT_API_KEY); it is off until then. Text only.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack; self-hosted when an endpoint is set
